utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is case number IT-95-14/1, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I turn to the Office of the Prosecutor now. Can we please have the appearances this morning for the International Criminal Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda, Mr. Marchesiello, Ms. Sutherland and Ms. Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is Goran Mikulicic; together, along with my colleague, Mr. Joka, we represent the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Let us now resume the hearing, and we have another witness of the Prosecution, I believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is correct. I call Mr. Junhov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: May we enquire if that is the last witness for the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not the last for the week; we have two for tomorrow, but it is the only witness for today, I am afraid. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You are going to read the solemn declaration given to you by the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: And, please, answer the questions that the Prosecutor, Mr. Niemann, I think, is going to put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. TORBJORN JUNHOV

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you state your full name for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Torbjorn Junhov.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born 2nd August 1937.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of Sweden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, in 1993, did you join the European Community Monitoring Mission to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And do you remember when, in 1993, you joined the Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Sweden on 23 March and stayed for the first week in Zagreb at the headquarters of the ECMM for a kind of introduction training and then I left Zagreb via Split and was appointed a Monitor in the regional centre in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you have any specific tasks when you were appointed in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started as a newcomer -- I started as a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the Busovaca Joint Commission -- what was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was some kind of a cooperation, organisation between the two parties, the Muslims and the Croats, in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how were the parties represented at this Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were represented by local military commanders, brigade commanders, and even local politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of the Busovaca Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose was to establish law and order and to establish a cease-fire, withdrawal of troops and reunification of the community -- how you call it -- civil part of the community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Restoration of the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And when was it first set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was set up before I arrived and I think it was set up during the winter 1991-92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And winter 1991-92?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- perhaps it is spring time 1992. I do not remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. And what position did you have on the Busovaca Commission when you were appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first weeks I was, so to say, an ordinary Monitor -- I was a member of the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did the Commission meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did the Commission meet -- where did you meet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meetings were held at different places, depending on the agenda or the meeting. Sometimes it was in the municipality meeting in the centre of Busovaca and sometimes it was at some of the UN peace-keeping forces or UNPROFOR camps and sometimes it was out in a village where trouble was going on, so we moved around in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the matters discussed at the commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first period, it was to establish a cease-fire and to withdraw troops from the area, to fill up trenches, and to reorganise the civilian government in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And fill up trenches where -- where did you have to fill up trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most discussion was the main road from Busovaca, first, towards Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to filling up trenches, did you become involved in other issues apart from those that you have mentioned, such as withdrawal of troops and filling up of trenches and reorganising of the civilian government -- did you become involved in anything else other than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, there were very often discussions about who should start and why, and where to start, and when we tried to push the local commanders to take initiatives they always had some excuses not to do it -- at least not today, perhaps next week. It was very often a discussion of missing people from the local area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how did these issues about missing people -- how did they arise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They arose at the meeting when we tried to push them to start doing something, they said -- very often they said, "Okay, we see the need for that, but we do not do it before we get an answer to where is our missing people".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how did you go about resolving that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not, of course, one of our most important tasks, so we cooperated in all these questions with the ICRC organisation that had an officer in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the cooperation that you had with the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very often, we -- the ICRC took part sometimes in the committee meetings and if we got information during our work in the field -- we got, for instance, lists of missing people -- we handed it over to the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And how did you go about resolving the question of where these missing people were? What did you do in order to resolve this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no systematic work from our side, because we did not regard it as a main task for us in the very beginning, but, of course, we asked people when we were travelling around in the area, "Do you know something about some detainees, people, here, or some prisoners?", or something like that, and we tried to track where they could possibly be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you believe that these people were being detained in some sort of detention centres in various locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we got -- later on, we spotted such places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And can you remember the names of some of these places now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were -- the most -- the biggest one was to Kacuni prison in the north of Busovaca at the main road in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other camps also, with smaller groups of people held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And just going back for a moment, you said that you started off just as an ordinary observer with the Busovaca Commission. Did you later take a more formal appointment on that Commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after a couple or three weeks, I was appointed chairman of the committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also mentioned the fact that you were -- part of the issues involved were the filling of trenches. So far as you are aware, did you ever succeed in getting these trenches filled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, apart from these issues that you discussed, was there any other role that you performed -- the implementation of any other programme that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number of cease-fire agreements established on the top level -- the governmental level in Bosnia Herzegovina, signed by the top commanders of HVO and BiH, and we received these agreements with a task to take part in the implementation -- to look to -- that the agreement were known by local commanders and that they were, so to say -- I am missing the word -- to implement the agreement on the local level. Every single battalion group in the area, or deployed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about international initiatives, did you have any involvement with those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what way -- in the international --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: International initiatives, were you involved in any way in the implementation of international initiatives that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later on, in May and June, I was appointed -- the Busovaca Joint Commission broke down and it was replaced by a joint operational command located in Travnik and, during that period, I was also appointed as -- from the ECMM, part of the responsibility -- I was appointed as responsible for implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan in province number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan was -- in my personal opinion, it was a kind of desk job from New York, or the United Nations headquarters and there was obviously no response on the local level to implement it. They regarded the borders as unnatural -- there were areas with no natural context that were brought together and other natural areas that belonged to each other were separated by new borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you encounter difficulties in the implementation of this plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was it because of these factors that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the implementation of the plan ultimately successful, or did it fail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a big failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just want to take you back to these meetings that you had, particularly when you were in the Busovaca Commission. Can you remember the names of some of the persons that you met at these particular meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I find it very hard to remember names, but one frequent member of the committee was an HVO brigade commander in Busovaca and his opposite number from the Muslim side was -- he introduced himself as President of the War Presidency and he had his headquarters in Kacuni, south of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what his name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to go and visit one of these camps that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The reason for that was that we had a meeting in Zenica with the ICRC, and we were presented with a problem that, according to the ICRC people, was some kind of root to all problems in the area, and that was persons -- international or foreigners -- that were detained in the area -- Muslim people that were detained and the ICRC had no track at all of it, and, as a member of the Busovaca Joint Commission, I was asked by the ICRC to make a check in the area if there might be some camp or prison where these so-called muhajedeen could be placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we asked the local people in Busovaca if there was any camp or prison there, and the answer was positive, there is a prison in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When they said there was a prison in Kaonik, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went there to visit it, and to see what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you on your own, or were you in the company of others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were -- the Monitor team, I had a German colleague, his name was Dieter Schnelsmith and then we had a local interpreter, and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to Kaonik, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we spotted the place, and turned in on the main road into the area, there was a guard and we were stopped at the gate, and we presented our documents that were freedom of movement in the area, but we were stopped and the guard told us he had no authority to let us in. So then I went back to the police station in Busovaca and took contact with the chief of the police and told him I wanted to go to the prison, and I wanted to be let in there and I wanted to see what is in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was this, approximately what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 1st April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened when you went back to the police in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wrote permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he ask you why you wanted to see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but of course he was not -- in the first place, he was not so willing to -- "what should you do there?". I said, "I just want to see the place, what is going on there and that is part of my mission as a Monitor."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he ultimately -- I think you said he gave you permission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was no long discussion, just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened -- what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I then got a paper from him and I went back to the camp and presented it at the guard and they let us in, and drove up the road to the first building, and stopped there and there was -- I do not remember exactly if there were people from the guard that escorted us up there, or if there were people there already that met us, but we were met by some soldiers and I told them, "I want to go in this building and see what is going on."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were the soldiers dressed, can you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As ordinary soldiers, some parts of camouflage uniforms and some civilian clothes -- it was a mixture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did they have any insignia or anything that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them had the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened when you said you wanted to go inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I was let in, and I was met by a person that introduced himself as -- I do not remember if he said he was in charge of the prison, or he was a commandant, but he was obviously, in my opinion, the responsible person for the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to describe the person that you met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us say he was about 40 years old, not so high, 165, 170 (indicating), a bit fat or round, and he spoke no English, so we had to communicate by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, when you met this person, did he give his name or do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, when you met this person, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took us into the building and he had some kind of office in there, with a desk and he had a file and he asked us to identify ourselves, and he noted our ID card number that we presented him with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you were there, did you take some photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at this photograph that I now show you, please, and there is one for your Honours and one for the Defence -- I think the Defence has their copy. Might this photograph be placed on the ELMO once it is given the next Prosecution exhibit number in order, if your Honours please. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is document number 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I want you to leave that on the screen because that can then be seen by all of us. I want you to tell me, firstly, do you recognise the photograph you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have taken it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you take it -- was that the day you went there, that you have just been describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is it a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first building -- the main entrance road is up here, and this is the first building and there is another building further off there. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the witness is pointing to the far right-hand side of the photograph looking at the photograph, in the middle section of the right-hand side. Did you gain an impression of what this building could have been -- its past history, when you looked at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It looks very like the Swedish army's ordinary munitions stores.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you have that opinion, that it looked like a munitions store, and I think you said a Swedish army one, but why did you have that impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The size of the building. It is a concrete building, there is a loading ramp along the building for the handling of heavy equipment to load off and load on trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness is pointing to the front of the building immediately behind the car that appears in the forefront of the building -- the Audi car, I think it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And a quite big door, you could open the door and my impression was it was used to handle big, heavy equipment with a fork truck or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that, if your Honours please. When you went inside the building, of course, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building was, so to say, parted by a corridor along the building, and a number of doors on each side of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what did those doors appear to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were -- seemed solid and they were locked, and it appeared to be cells for prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When -- okay, I tender that. That may now be handed up. When you went inside this building - and you said you had a meeting with the person who described himself as either being in command, or the commander, and he took some details from you -- then what happened after the details were taken, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I told him that I would like to get an opinion of what kind of facility this was, and I asked him, "What is it?". He said it was a prison. "What kind of prisoners do you have here?"; "Ordinary criminals" was the answer. Then I said, "Do you mind if I look into the cells here?"; "No, you are free to choose" he said. I pointed at one door and it was open, and inside there was one single man -- hard to say his age -- between 20 and 30 -- and I asked him, "Why are you locked up here?", and he said he was sentenced to 10 years prison for murder and then I turned around and pointed at a door at the other side of the corridor, "Could you open this door, please?", and it was open and inside there, there were five persons in the same cell. I asked, "What kind of people are these?"; "They are arrested"; "For what?" And also, "They are foreigners and they are arrested because they were armed and they had no passports or documents that were legal for a visit in the area". And then I asked the persons in the cell, "Where do you come from? What is your mission here?". They described themselves as missionaries, they were supporting the Muslim people in Bosnia, and they were from different, other Arab or other Muslim countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are these the people -- were these the people that you had thought were the muhajedeen that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ask them why they were in prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I asked them, "Why are you in prison here?", and some of them said, "I do not know, I have done nothing criminal. I was just arrested and put in here."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you determine -- did you ascertain whether or not they had been charged with any crime, or whether they had stood trial for any crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not accused for any crimes, according to their own statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And now looking at the photograph that I show you -- (Handed). There is one for your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just again looking at the document that appears on the machine beside you there, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my own photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is it a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is taken from the entrance door to the cell and these are the five so-called muhajedeen. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And these are the people that you had the conversation with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they tell you where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I asked them and now I do not remember which individual it was, from which country they were, but if I may, I have some notes in my diary --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you asking their Honours' permission to let you to refer to those notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness have permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them was from Egypt, another from Pakistan, a third one from Tunisia and another one from Algeria, according to my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph. Did you manage to observe what conditions were like in this particular camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I refer to the standard of a Swedish person, it was not acceptable to keep people in such conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because these five persons, they sat in one cell. They had a common bed, there were no toilets, there was no possibility to wash yourself, and medical care was non-existent, according to the people I talked to, and there were also bad food -- bad eating.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at this next photograph that I show you -- perhaps you might tell me what that is. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, can you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- in the right-hand corner in the cell (indicating) and it is what the prisoners call -- "it is our kitchen". There were some casseroles or -- where they got their meal, their food, but there was no heating on this -- it was only a desk or what you could call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With some drawers in and packets of biscuits -- very simple food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that. You described that there was a bed. Did you manage to look at the bed and determine what sort of a bed it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one common bed alongside one wall in the cell, and they had to sleep together in the same bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you see whether it had a mattress or whether it had a base or anything of that nature -- you may not have seen that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was some kind of mattress, a dirty one, with some blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned there was no toilet in the cells. Did you see toilets anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I did not ask for it, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the conditions in the cells appear clean, or were they dirty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dirty -- very dirty and it was a smell that was awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the prisoners themselves, did they appear clean or dirty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dirty -- very dirty, unshaven, and dirty clothes. I do not think they have had a shower for the last month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then discuss this question with the person who had identified himself as the commander or the person in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- perhaps I can describe it as a bit upset over the conditions in the prison, so I asked him about his knowledge of the Geneva Conventions and he told me he knew it and he had a copy of it in his desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So he knew about the Geneva Conventions and he had a copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and he told me, but, in my opinion, the conditions in the prison were not in accordance with the Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after you had spoken to these five gentlemen that have been depicted in the photograph, what did you do then, and the commander -- what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then, in my opinion, I have fulfilled my mission -- I have found these five persons that I was looking for, so I said, "Thank you" and I left the place and delivered a message to the ICRC that these five people are in the Kaonik prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you have occasion to then discuss the issue of the Kaonik prison again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now and then during my whole period in Central Bosnia, there was discussions about missing people and we were -- at almost every meeting we were presented with lists from both sides of missing people. Sometimes it was just a scrap of paper with a written name, or sometimes it was long lists of up to 30, 40, 50 names from different areas in the Central Bosnia. ECMM had no means whatsoever to handle all this information, so we consequently handed it over to the ICRC because they had the computer systems and could track every individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But did you have a meeting about the prisons on 7 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I would like to contact my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7 April?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 7 April there was a meeting with the coordination committee. It was a meeting with the coordination committee in an UN camp in Kakanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, there is a date appearing, 4 April 1993. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 4 April? I do not understand what you are asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might rephrase the question. We were talking about this meeting at Kakanje of the coordinating committee on 7 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I mention the fact in your statement you say it is 4 April. Is that a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the photographs I now show you? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what is it a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is from the coordination committee meeting in Kakanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, looking at the photograph, can you identify any of the people that you see photographed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the meeting was chaired by the head of the regional centre in Zenica from ECMM, the French ambassador Jean-Pierre Tibo. On his left-hand side, there is Colonel Blaskic from HVO and, on his right-hand side, there is Major -- Lieutenant General Hasihasinovic, who was a commander of the III Army Corps BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was the III Army Corps BiH headquartered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the iron factory in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where was the HVO headquartered that Colonel Blaskic was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His headquarters were in Hotel Vitez in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you see the insignia on the arm of Colonel Blaskic? Is that the sort of insignia you saw at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was the normal HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the gentleman on the far end -- either far end, one next to Colonel Blaskic, do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was -- as I understood it, it was some kind of political adviser or political assistant to the Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the gentleman on the other far end, the opposite far end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the opposite number from the Muslim side. I do not remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph, your Honours. Was there any discussion about the Kaonik prison at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Among all other items on the agenda there was a question from the Muslim side about the Kaonik prison and it was a request or a demand to get this prison examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Examined by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or inspected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Examined or inspected by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to a decision in the committee, the task was given to the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the ICRC were regularly taking part in these kind of meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the response from Colonel Blaskic and the HVO in relation to this request for an inspection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no clear memory of that. I do not remember -- there was some kind of refusal -- there was obviously some suspicion, attitude from the Muslim side that there was something going on in Kaonik that they did not know. That was my opinion of the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was there any particular demand made at the meeting with respect to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that, and I have no notes of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the five prisoners that you had seen before, had they been released at that stage, or had they been discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was not -- as far as I remember, there were no discussions in detail at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, was there then a later meeting in relation to release of prisoners from Kaonik prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was later on, when, according to my opinion, when the Muslim side did not experience some success in the request to get these people out -- they tried to create some pressure on the Croat side, and that started with a kidnapping of a Croat Colonel. He had been in a meeting in our headquarters in Zenica and when he left the meeting he was kidnapped by some Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then a couple of days after that kidnapping, there was a visitor to our headquarters in Zenica with a videotape, and he asked us to present this videotape to the HVO headquarters, and we did so, and it was an appeal from this kidnapped Colonel to establish some kind of exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was it effective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision from the HVO headquarters was, "We do not deal with these kind of people."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And who made that decision, did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were presented with the decision in the headquarters in the Hotel Vitez, and I do not know which person -- individual person -- had taken the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then, another day after that, there were a new -- of course, we delivered the result to the Muslim side, and then, after another couple of days, there was a new kidnapping in the Travnik area, and a group of Croat officers were kidnapped and they were reported missing within the Croat organisation, and, after another couple of days, we had a new visitor with a new videotape, with all these four or five officers appealing to his -- to their commander to make a deal with the Muslims and exchange the prisoners. After we had presented this tape in the Hotel Vitez, there was a decision, "Okay, let us go for it".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was a date set when this would occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist you. Would you look at your diary on 9 May 1993 and see if that rings a bell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 9th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a note here, "Please release the civil members of the government in Kaonik", but that was another case -- that was the politician from Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, I think there was a meeting on 9 May. Perhaps I can assist you a bit more. Can you go to 16 May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 16th? 16 May, there was an exchange of prisoners in the Vitez area, but that has nothing to do with the so-called muhajedeen release. Okay. That is here -- the release was planned during the week before this date and then it was carried out in cooperation between the UN BRITBAT and the ECMM and it took place in what we called the blue factory. It was a factory on the road in the Lasva Valley -- if you travel from Zenica up to Busovaca, just before the road junction to Busovaca, there was a blue factory and there we had an exchange point of these muhajedeen and they were transported there from different places in the Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Those notes you are reading from, when did you make them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you make those notes that you are reading from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same day, and the ICRC were also represented and took notes of -- identification notes of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So these included the people that you had seen in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there ever an exchange at the Kaonik camp that you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was another exchange of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were so many -- I have a photo of a release of prisoners from Kaonik. Perhaps you could refer to my statement -- it is easier for me to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You take your time and look through your diary and see if you can find it. (Pause). To speed it up a bit, can you just see what you were doing on 17 May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 17th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 17 and, while you are doing that, your Honours, perhaps I might show the witness another photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a short note, "Busovaca local commission meeting at 10 o'clock, release of detained persons and prisoners" -- a very short notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just looking at this photograph you are now shown -- put away your diary for a moment and just look at this photograph, if you would. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is exhibit number 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is also a photo that I have taken myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you turn the photo over, please? Do you see writing that appears on the back of that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what does it say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Release of detained persons from Kaonik prison on 17 May 1993. The detainees are Muslims from the area."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you write that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wrote it in October last year, when I was talking to the -- to your investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn the photograph back over again, please. Are you able to say what it is a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same building as before, and the main entrance into the prison and the people who are lined up in front of the building, they were these detained Muslim people -- local people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, so far as you were concerned, were these people civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, apart from the people that are lined up there, can you point to and recognise any other persons there, other than prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this man, he is my team mate (indicating), a Dutch Monitor, Hank Morsenk. This girl was from ICRC, and this guy was also a servant from ICRC. There is some other representatives here -- might be representatives from the Medicine Sans Frontiers, and here is some Croat soldier or guard -- this is also Croat people working in the prison here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And so the Croat person working in the prison here that you have just referred to, for the sake of identification, is the second male standing on the platform on the right-hand side of the photograph looking at the photograph. What were these people lined up for -- what were they doing here, on this date, 17 May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were detained without -- no reason at all, just for some kind of bargain chips, or something to have to exchange to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why are they lined up here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For identification and to book them off the ICRC's lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to them, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this identification procedure, they were released and the ICRC had some buses that transported them back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you actually see where they were taken to yourself, or is that just something that you had learned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it myself -- I saw them enter the bus, but where the journey ended, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But the journey was supervised by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, after they had entered the bus, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I continued my job as a Monitor. I noted, okay, this business is okay, it is fixed, and then we take the next item.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any discussion with these people at all, or were you just there present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I talked to some of them, to get an opinion of why are they here, and they had been picked up in the area around Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In their homes, or where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what sort of condition did they appear to be in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were -- of course, they were happy to be released, but I do not know how long they had been here, but they did not seem to be in too bad condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph now, if your Honours please. When you say you had discussions regarding the release of these prisoners and, in particular, the prisoners from -- the international prisoners from Egypt and other places, can you recall who you had discussions with at this stage, or was it just representatives from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the names of people, but there were different kinds of meetings -- the so-called top level meeting that was chaired by our head of regional centre, and there were -- on this meeting there were also the commanders from both sides, and then we had meetings on the level below that, with the local commander, brigade commanders and local politicians, local police chiefs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic, if I may. During the course of the period of time that you were there as an European Monitor, and, in particular, during 1993, did you ever have occasion to visit Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Tomislavgrad is a small city situated on the road that we used when we entered Bosnia. It was some 20, 25 kilometres east of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is Tomislavgrad in Bosnia, or is it in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is just inside the border on the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in there, did you observe any troops in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I visited Tomislavgrad four or five times and my impression was that it was always a lot of troops there, and there were -- my idea as a professional officer was that Tomislavgrad was used as some kind of a refreshing of units or units that had been in fighting that were withdrawn for resting and freshening up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And could you determine what particular units they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not make notes of that, but it was, of course, HVO soldiers or HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it only HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not see any others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I see. When you were in Bosnia, did you -- Bosnia Herzegovina, did you see any other Croatian, if I might call it, military units other than HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were other groups of -- I do not know if it is adequate to call them military units, but at least groups of soldiers with black uniforms and a mark -- with "HOS".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what were your dealings with the HOS in terms of -- where did you see them and what did you do when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw them now and then on different locations in the whole area of Central Bosnia, and our experience as Monitors was that, when these groups were out -- were seen somewhere, we had a joke -- we said, "You can bet there will be trouble" when you saw these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did that prove to be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, did you yourself have dealings, personally, with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I met them -- our basic view of it was to avoid them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were, in our opinion, not trustworthy and they were behaving brutally and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And why did you feel they were not trustworthy so far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason for that was, of course, what we heard from other people and other Monitors who had been in trouble with them, and there was some kind of a gentlemen's agreement within the Monitor corps -- do not go in contact with these people, try to avoid them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about HV, did you ever see anyone wearing HV insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think that this would be a good time for a 20-minute break before we begin with the cross-examination. Therefore, we will adjourn for 20 minutes. (11.14am) (A short break) (11.35am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sir, now you are going to be asked questions by the Defence. Up until now you have been asked questions by the Prosecutor, so the Defence counsel, Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Torbjorn Junhov. I apologise if I mispronounce your name. Is it Torbjorn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Junhov?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is the correct pronunciation, I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone be put on for the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Mikulicic and I represent the Defence in this case. I will pose several questions and I would like you to answer to them, to your best memory. Mr. Junhov, you said how you came to the area of Central Bosnia and how you became a member and then the president of the joint mission in Busovaca. You told us that, as a member and then the president of this Commission, you had meetings with local military and civilian persons including their superiors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, could you please take a look at the person sitting behind me, and for the record I am pointing to the accused Zlatko Aleksovski; tell us, was this man ever, as you recollect, was he ever present at any meetings in Busovaca which you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this the person -- could you raise your hand? (Indicates to the accused). (Accused stands).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no memory that I met this guy at the prison, but I recognise his face, from probably some other occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, I did not ask about the prison; I was asking about the meetings of the joint commission in Busovaca. To your recollection, did this man ever attend any of these meetings at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have met this man -- I recognise his face, but I cannot say exactly when and where, because it is five years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, according to the notes which you took from these joint meetings in Busovaca, would you be able to recall that one of the persons attending these meetings would be someone named Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Junhov, what was your motivation, or what was your objective, what was the goal of your visit to the Kaonik facility near Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason for the first visit was to look for these persons that ICRC had asked us to look for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber which persons you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the regional office of ICRC in Zenica, and there were a lot of people there, but at this very moment, if I remember correctly, it was a French gentleman -- I do not remember his name -- and he was head of ICRC missions in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise -- we had a misunderstanding. When I asked about persons, I was thinking about persons in Kaonik that you went to try to find out, who were in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were these five muhajedeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described to us the events during your first visit to Kaonik when the guard did not admit you into the compound. Can you tell us, how was the guard dressed? Was he dressed in civilian clothes, or was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost all the soldiers, they had mixed uniforms and civilian clothes. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that after that you went to get a permit, which would enable you to enter the compound; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you went to get this permit at the police station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you received this permit at the police station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, how do you explain this situation: a soldier does not allow you to enter this compound and then the civilian police issue you a permit to enter it? What is your explanation of this seemingly absurd situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly the discussions with the guards, but I asked to whom could I appeal to get permission to enter the area and he referred to the chief of police in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but we are talking about the chief of the civilian police here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went to the police station in central Busovaca and I cannot identify these people if they are civilian police or military police, or what kind, but this officer had his office in the police station in central Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Junhov, how long were you at Kaonik that first time -- how long did your visit take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think from the first attempt to get in there until I left, it was about one and a half hours, something like that -- perhaps two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, this time includes your trip to Busovaca to get this permit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but how much time did you spend in the facility itself once you received the permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked to the commander for about a quarter of an hour, and then my discussions with the muhajedeen was about 20 minutes or maximum half an hour, so I would say I spent totally just around one hour in the building, or perhaps a little bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where you conducted your conversation with the commander, as you call him -- the prison commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered the building, he had his office in the right-hand end, so to say, of the building, and I do not remember if it was in a separate room, or if his desk was in the corridor, but it was at the right-hand end in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. At that time, how many cells did you review in this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only these two that I referred to -- the first one with the man who was sentenced for murder, and then, just by random, I happened to point at the right door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, when you described the conditions at the prison, at Kaonik, you -- and I quote you -- comparing it to the Swedish standards, these conditions were not good?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, since we are talking about the Swedish standards here, which is what you used when judging the conditions there, can you tell the Trial Chamber and all of us what were the roads like, the infrastructure, the homes, the supply at that location in comparison to the Swedish standards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, it was not the Swedish standard at all, because it was a lot of damage in the whole society -- of course it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, you mentioned that the largest camp at that time was the camp in Kacuni; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not remember I said it was the largest one, but it was -- compared to some other places where the detained persons were held, it was -- seems to be a big one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is what I was referring to -- I apologise if I misinterpreted what you had said. Under whose control was this camp in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my opinion, the commander at the Kacuni prison was under the command of the police -- chief of police in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- and we are talking now about the ethnic background -- which persons were imprisoned in this camp in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question -- which person, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, I am going to ask you directly: who were the prisoners at Kacuni, and in terms of either their belonging to a military organisation or to their ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first one --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I object? It is not really an objection -- it is just a clarification. I am not sure whether counsel is asking about the place that I mentioned and what the witness mentioned in chief -- Kacuni or Kakanje -- I think there might be two places. I think it might be helpful if that was clarified, because there may be some confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, can you clarify your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Maybe it would be the simplest thing if I could rephrase my questions in order to avoid any kind of misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Junhov, apart from Kaonik, how many similar facilities of similar -- with similar purpose did you visit during your stay in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kaonik prison was, so to say, permanent. As I got it, it was more or less a permanent prison, but other places we saw were temporary. They were local school buildings or basements in ordinary houses that were used to, so to say, store detained persons and it was both on the Croat and Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Can you tell us what were the conditions in these other facilities which you just mentioned in comparison to the conditions at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was -- it is hard to separate them, but it was not acceptable conditions anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were the conditions which you found at Kaonik, which were below the Swedish standards -- were they also below the conditions at these other facilities which you also saw and mentioned? Were they poorer or were they more or less the same as in these other locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to separate them, because it was far below any acceptable standard anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understood that, but, in relation to what else you saw in Central Bosnia, can you make any kind of comparison in that respect, because this entire case is highlighting the situation in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I understand your point to the question. The standard -- average standard everywhere, even for civilians -- everybody was of course affected by the hostilities, and the standard in Kaonik prison was -- I cannot say it was worse than other places I saw, but I -- this was also, you should remember, my first visit to such a facility and my reaction was very strong, that it was very, very bad standard in all aspects in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Junhov, you showed us photographs which you took -- which you personally took on that occasion at Kaonik. Did you take some other photographs at other facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have photographs, for instance, from the HVO military prison in Kiseljak and I have photographs from a Muslim detainee camp -- I do not remember the name -- it was on the road from Busovaca to Kiseljak. It was a gas factory -- we also released detained persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Since we are talking about photographs, I would like to request that the usher puts the exhibit number 67 on the ELMO, please. Can you identify the object that is hanging from the wall on the left-hand -- upper left-hand corner of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a towel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on to the exhibit number 68. (Handed). Correct me if I am wrong, Mr. Junhov, but I believe that the object which was -- of which you took a photograph here was described as some kind of stove -- cooking stove?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not -- there was no heating equipment here. It was only -- I do not know the English name of it. It is a chest of drawers where they had their food. This is some casserole with water and it was -- I do not know if it was a coffee pan or what it was (indicating) and some biscuit package.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Junhov, does this mean that these persons -- and we are talking about this object, is from the cells in which the muhajedeen were staying; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, inside this cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that these persons actually prepared their own food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if they were served food, or -- but this is not possible to prepare food, or to cook food. It was, as I understand, some kind of place where they were served the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now place the photograph number 70 on the ELMO, please? Mr. Junhov, looking at this photograph, in the upper part to the right you identified the second person from the right as one of the guards in Kaonik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you, are you sure that it is a guard, or did you think it was a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not introduce himself, so I do not know, but there were several persons even inside and outside that were dressed in almost the same style, and some of them were armed and some were not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the persons you are referring to have any military insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as you can see from this picture. Normally, they had insignia on the left arm, or on the pocket on the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, thank you. We can remove the photograph now from the ELMO. Mr. Junhov, you said that you spent some time talking to someone you described as the prison commander. Do you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was dressed in the same fashion as these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he had any military insignia on his clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember that, but my opinion of the person was that he was a military person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what did you conclude that, when you do not recall him having any military insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had at least some parts of a uniform -- a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, but a moment ago you told us that, in those days, in that area, there were many people wearing parts of military uniforms -- that is true, even though they were civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but how do you separate civilians from military persons when they are partly in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is what I am trying to ask you. How did you come to the conclusion that he was a military person when he had no insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is of course hard to say, but it is an impression you get when you meet the people and you talk to him, and his way to behave and so on. There was no doubt about that he was in charge -- he was responsible for at least this building, and I had the opinion that he was responsible for the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, it seems to me that you mentioned that you spoke to the commander, as you call him, in his office, which was on the right-hand side of the building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you, of course bearing in mind the former standards you referred to, that is, the Swedish standards, could you describe to me the standard of equipment in that office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was an ordinary desk with a chair and some files and a telephone on the table, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How would you describe that office, using as your yardstick the standard you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a very, very simple office, I would say. It was -- perhaps it is more appropriate to call it a working place for desk work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice at the entrance of the building you went into or at the door of this office any kind of inscription, any kind of board -- do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a number above the entrance door, outside the building, and you saw it in the picture -- it was number 12, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is what can be seen on the photograph, thank you. And, just briefly, Mr. Junhov, you mentioned in your testimony the HOS military units. Would you tell us whether you know under whose command those units were, or, rather, those people that you saw with the HOS insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, that is of course hard to say, because we avoided discussions with these people, but I take it for natural that, since they were military units, they must have been under the command of the commander of Central Bosnia, because they acted in his area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, just for a moment let us go back to your visit to Kaonik and the conversation you had with the five muhajedeen that you told us about. Did you notice on those men any signs of injuries, the effects of blows, or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not notice that, and I have also mentioned that they were unshaven, beard, they had full covering of clothes, so almost the only thing you saw of them was their eyes and ears, and I saw no sign of mistreating, or beating, except that they were very dirty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, did they complain to you that they were being beaten or mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were complaining that they had no medical care; they were complaining of the hygienic -- or what you call it -- they could not keep themselves clean, because they had not access to a bathroom, showers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But did they complain that anyone was physically abusing them or beating them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not beating them -- nobody -- none of them said they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could your Honours just excuse me for a moment, please? Nothing in re-examination, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, from your evidence, you gave me the impression that you are well versed with the prison conditions in Sweden. May I know what your profession was before you were appointed a Monitor by ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a retired Colonel from the Swedish air force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Junhov, I should like to ask you a question: if I understood well, you went to Kaonik twice, and speaking of the distinction between military and civilian persons, if I understood well, you said that it was easy to make a distinction and, also, the distinction between guards and soldiers in the Kaonik prison. Could you make a distinction between the guards and the soldiers in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards and the soldiers, that is similar or equal, in my opinion. The guards were dressed as, -- in my opinion, it was military personnel. They had uniforms and weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, you did not see any external signs which would allow you to make a distinction between the military and the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, this was a prison after all. There was no possibility for you to distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not notice it. It was not, in my opinion, a remarkable experience that military personnel -- it is hard to make a discrimination between -- people acting as policemen or soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But was it easy for you to distinguish between military people and civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes it was, and sometimes not. I can say that I visited a lot of police stations in the Central Bosnia, and you went into the police station, you could meet with a man in a camouflage uniform and armed as a soldier and there were also people dressed in other, so to say, strictly police uniforms. I do not know if the Police Forces were reinforced by military police. I did not know the organisation correctly, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Junhov. You have just completed your testimony here at the International Criminal Tribunal, and we wish to thank you for coming and we wish you a happy journey to your country. Mr. Niemann, you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I ask one question arising out of what your Honour was asking the witness? It may help clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, with the same possibility for the Defence to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In your travels around Bosnia Herzegovina when you were there as a Monitor and other than the time when you were in Kaonik, did you see other soldiers on the Croatian side who were dressed in a similar fashion to the people that you saw at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you wish to put a question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour, we have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, I think we have finished our work for this morning. I believe there are no more witnesses, and we will have two, I think, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, we are going to adjourn for today, and we will meet again here tomorrow. Until tomorrow then. (12.15pm)
